title: In situ  gelling polymeric hemostatic powders: molecular design, interfacial mechanics and translational outlook of dry-to-wet functional interfaces
content: Rapid control of hemorrhage in complex, deep-seated, and non-compressible scenarios remains a critical challenge in both surgical and battlefield settings. Conventional hemostats face an intrinsic physicochemical dilemma. Powders offer superior conformability but lack resistance to washout under high-flow conditions, whereas pre-formed hydrogels achieve robust tissue sealing yet cannot be precisely delivered to irregular wound beds. Against this backdrop, in situ gelling polymeric hemostatic powders have emerged as a transformative strategy. By leveraging blood-triggered, ultrafast powder-to-gel phase transition kinetics, these materials realize on-demand switching from a dry, flowable state for delivery to a wet, cohesive state for sealing, reconciling the two sets of mutually exclusive functional demands. This review establishes a comprehensive research framework covering molecular design, interfacial mechanics, and organ-specific material optimization. We first systematically dissect core crosslinking mechanisms and multicomponent synergistic principles that underpin rapid in situ gelation. Subsequently, we analyze tailored material engineering strategies for harsh physiological microenvironments, including acidic gastrointestinal lesions, high-pressure arterial hemorrhage, and deep traumatic cavities. Finally, we identify the remaining cross-cutting challenges and outline future directions, including stimulus-responsive precision crosslinking, artificial-intelligence-assisted molecular design, and multifunctional integration, toward an active hemostatic system that senses the bleeding microenvironment and degrades with programmed kinetics.
